utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning to you, too, Madam Registrar. If you could call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is the case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All the accused are here. From the Defence teams, the position is as it was yesterday; that is Mr. Ostojic and Mr. Bourgon are absent. Prosecution, we have Mr. McCloskey, Mr. Thayer, Mr. Nicholls, Ms. Soljan. All right. I don't see the witness in the courtroom. Why don't we finish with the witness first and then deal with other matters afterwards. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, I hear that the witness may be on for another couple of hours on cross and perhaps redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that --

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And the reason I was here was because of a -- the next witness, and Mr. Haynes apparently has made a -- has started discussing a challenge to the protective measures. I would prefer to be with the witness trying to prepare, but I have had a chance to briefly speak with Mr. Haynes; and if possible, I wouldn't expect to take up much of your time this morning. Any legal discussion about protective, Mr. Nicholls is prepared for; but in speaking with Mr. Haynes, while we have some very different ideas about this, we actually have some things in common that I think we would like to share with you. It won't take long, I hope not more than ten or 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes, Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. I just would like to let the Chamber know that it's not just Peter Haynes who has some issues with these protective measures issues with the next witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, Mr. Meek. All right. Then we start with these issues. Whoever wishes to go first. Mr. McCloskey? Mr. Haynes? I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And, Mr. President, if we could go into private session for these issues?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: I'm not unhappy. There is a short procedural matter that I would like to raise, happy to do it now. Yesterday, the Trial Chamber rendered an oral decision in relation to the cross-examination issue, and directed us to Judge Kwon's decision in the Milosevic case dated the 29th of April 2004. That we have found and we have all seen. What we would quite like to view is the confidential decision of the other members of that Chamber dated the 28th of January 2004. Now, Your Honour, we are quite content. I have, obviously, no idea what is in that decision, and it may deal with a whole range of issues. Coincidentally, it's very close to the decisions that have just been alluded to in private session, but I assume that is a coincidence. We would be quite content for one of Your Honour's Legal Officers to go through that decision and excise or redact those parts that don't relate to the issue that we are interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think we will need to do that, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The reason you are interested in seeing that is to look for any reasoning for the majority's view?

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Correct. I should make it clear we are contemplating a certification application. That's why we would like to see the majority view.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think I can fairly say that, but unfortunately there is none.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: There is none in it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There is none.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is conspicuously absent and you can take our word for it because I ordered a copy this morning. So we went through it, not the we did not believe Judge Kwon, but it is conspicuously absent.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I came into the courtroom happy and I'm now unhappy. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Yes. Now, this witness. Let's bring him in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: He will available immediately following this witness, Your Honour, or tomorrow morning, should we go all day with this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Good morning, sir. Can you hear me? Good morning to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning. I can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are going to finish with your cross-examination today. Thank you. Mr. Petrusic, your last words yesterday were that you weren't that sure that you would have further questions. If you do, please go ahead. If you don't, let us know that and Mr. Josse or Mr. Krgovic will take over.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETRUSIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. General Miletic's Defence has no further questions for this witness, and I would like to take this opportunity and apologise for exceeding the time for the cross-examination of this witness. Originally, I asked for less time, and I had to use more than I originally planned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Petrusic. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning. If you could introduce yourself with the witness, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, General. On behalf of General Gvero's Defence team, I'm going to have a few questions for you with regard to your testimony. My name is Dragan Krgovic, as you know. Since the two of us speak the same language, I would kindly ask you to proceed in the same way you did yesterday with Mr. Petrusic. After my question, please make a pause before you start giving your answer. General, sir, yesterday, in response to my learned friend Petrusic's question and the document that was shown to you, that was information from the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 5D431? Can we put -- can we see the second page of this document, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you can see that this liaison office for international military representatives, it is between the commander and the staff. According to my information, this department for liaison with international military representatives was directly linked to the office of the commander. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and this is exactly what I said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you also told us that in 1995, Colonel -- Lieutenant-Colonel Djurdjic was the head of that department.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that before that, it was Colonel Vidoje Magazin who was the head of that department, and I am sure that he was followed by Colonel Djurdjic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 5D438?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in answering my learned friend Petrusic's questions, you said that below the commander there should be another square containing another organ, the office. Could you please take a pen and put a square where the place of that organ was and to link it with the commander in the way explained to us that that organ should have been linked to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This square that should represent the office of the commander of the Main Staff of the Republika Srpska army should be here. [Marks] . Okay. Let's put a K for office and there are no other links there, and this square was excluded yesterday. This one containing the Chief of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in that. Could you just put this Office for Cooperation with Foreign Military Representatives there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but that office only had one person. Nobody else. And that person was in charge of liaising with foreign international military organisations, and he was also the secretary to the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in responding to my learned friend Petrusic's question, you explained the line before, with assistant commanders and chiefs of administrations. I want to ask you one thing. The assistant commanders were also chiefs of various branches. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Within the establishments, that's how they were not defined. They were not defined as chiefs of branches. They were just assistant commanders. The only person who was a deputy commander was the Chief of the Staff Sector.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But they were assistants for certain areas, for certain branches?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. I can even give you those areas, if you need me to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. Thank you very much. My question was of a general nature. If any of these assistants in charge of certain areas was unable to perform his duties, he would have a deputy to do that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it never happened that the assistants switched between the jobs? For example, General Gvero could not perform your duties. He could not discharge the duties of Tomic, who was in charge of the finances, or Tolimir's duties. That was not the principle that the army of Republika Srpska followed?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not a principle, and it did not happen in practice. The assistants never interfered with the competences and duties of a different assistant.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit number 6D7 -- I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Before we do that, could you please put your signature and today's date on this schematic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you want me to do it -- okay. [Marks] Today we are the 18th? I apologise, the 18th?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now see Exhibit number 6D7?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is a document, the Official Gazette of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please move to the next page and show it to the witness? Scroll down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a decision on the establishment of the state committee on cooperation with United Nations and international humanitarian organisations. You know that this committee existed in the course of 1995?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Various committees were established by the civilian authorities, and I knew that this one existed; although, I was not aware of its precise title, but now I can see it in the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Article 6 of this document? It says here that this committee is in charge of issuing permissions for the movement of convoys, the officials of the United Nations and humanitarian organisations. Do you agree with me, and would you say that it indeed functioned in that way at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's how it reads; and if it is written in here, then this is a legal obligation and everybody had to adhere by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at Article 1 of the decision to the right? Nikola Koljevic was appointed president of that committee.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. It says: "President of the state committee."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now scroll down a bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you now look at number 7? The person under number 7, Colonel Milos Djurdjic, the coordinator for the relationship between the committee and the Ministry of Defence and the Main Staff. It is the same Colonel Djurdjic that we have just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's correct. This is the same Colonel Djurdjic who was the aide de camp of the commander of the Main Staff. Did I say Supreme Commander? I meant the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit number 6D147? I apologise, Your Honours. This document is still not in e-court. We have distributed the document among the interpretation booths, and we have also provided our learned friends from the Prosecution with a copy of the document, which has been translated into English. Could you please place a copy on the ELMO? Could we have a B/C/S version on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, this is an instruction on contacts with international organisations that was issued by President Karadzic. Kindly look at bullet point 1 towards the end of the first page, and can you please read it aloud for all of us?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: "That's why I've decided, and the person who has decided is President Karadzic. All permits for the movement of humanitarian convoys, as well as the UNPROFOR supply convoys, will be issued in the office of the Supreme Commander. Prior to that, the office will obtain all the relevant opinions with regard to the matter at hand."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the counsel please repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Just for the record, I asked you whether this document confirms what I suggested to you about the competences with regard to humanitarian organisations and their convoys?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer need this document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. I wonder if the witness could help us in finding out who this Tant Mint U is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you hear Judge Kwon's question? Could you help us with this name, Tant Mint U? Are you familiar with it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But if I were to look at the document again, maybe I could make some inferences, if that would not be a waste of time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think the Prosecution wouldn't mind if you answered the question directly, if you have -- if you know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: If you know, Mr. Skrbic, of course, only if you know.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I repeat, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally, Your Honours, I don't know who is the person mentioned in this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness now be shown Exhibit P5?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday, you spoke in general terms about this document in response to Mr. Petrusic's questions, and now I'm going to ask you something else. My colleague Petrusic mentioned some titles and some topics in this document, and I'm going to go into some more detail. First of all, tell me, this is a directive issued by the Supreme Command. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I'm looking at is a copy of a directive issued by the Supreme Command, and the number of the directive is 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Supreme Command of Republika Srpska consisted of several persons at that time. I will tell you their names, and you will correct me if I'm wrong. First, Supreme Commander President Karadzic? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of Defence, General Subotic at the time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a while, he was the Minister of Defence, to be later replaced by Tomo Kovac, and Tomo Kovac was also part of the Supreme Command, so you could put it as Defence Minister.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Minister of Interior?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the Minister of Interior.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And no one from the Main Staff; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree but I want to emphasise that the commander of the Main [Realtime transcript read in error "plain"] Staff of the VRS was not a member of the Supreme Command; and since the commander wasn't a member, nobody else was a member either.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Just the transcript reads commander of the "plain" staff of the VRS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. No one is suggesting that it was plain. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you distinct between a directive from the Supreme Command and a directive from the command for operations that is drafted within the staff, the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not that I distinguish between the two. There is a distinction.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And yesterday, when you were responding to a question from my colleague, Mr. Petrusic, about directives, you were talking about directives drafted at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, about directives drafted at the Supreme Command, because in the Main Staff, or rather, in staffs, as far as I know, directives are not drafted at all. Orders are, commands and decisions. Directives are drafted only in Supreme Commands.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's what I wanted to hear from you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness page 10 of this directive? I think it's the next one, 00823177. Can we lower the page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, speaking of this document yesterday, you spoke about moral guidance and psychological support.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Petrusic asked you general questions, and you dealt only with subheadings and headings. You did not speak about the contents of this passage. In this passage, marked moral and psychological support, could you please read the last paragraph aloud: "Devote special attention," et cetera?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the last paragraph: "Devote special attention to the training and full combat readiness of all the air defence systems and units, train them and equip them for efficient fighting against all targets in the air space, especially with the combat units of the NATO alliance."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This passage deals with training and air defence systems. That is certainly not an area dealt with by the Sector for Moral Guidance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This does not fall under the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance by any criterion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It falls within the purview of Air Defence, and in part --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This item falls under the purview of the Administration for Air Defence. That's what we said yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That's why I stopped in mid-sentence, because I made a slip of the tongue. Now, read the next passage about other forms of support, aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "In applying other forms of support to combat activities, take all the measures stipulated by directive OP-6 with a proviso that the focus of logistical support in 1995 should be placed on the support of units that are planned to execute operations at the strategic level."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This passage that you have just read is a passage that does not fall within the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is about logistical support and, therefore, belongs to the Sector for Logistics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I showed you a couple of documents a moment ago dealing with jurisdiction over humanitarian convoys. Can you read the passage that begins with the words, "Through competent state and military authorities"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the previous paragraph that reads: "Through competent state and military authorities responsible for working with the UNPROFOR and humanitarian organisations, use planned and discreet restrictive granting of applications to reduce and restrict logistical support to the forces of the UNPROFOR in enclaves and the supply of material resources to Muslim population, and make them dependent on our goodwill, while at the same time avoiding condemnation by the international community and the public opinion in the world."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This passage relates precisely to the organ whose competences you explained a moment ago. That does not fall under the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly is not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we have back the previous page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, this first sentence, this first paragraph, read it aloud, please.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You mean 6.1?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "The state -- political and military leadership is hereby placed under the obligation to demonstrate maximum readiness initiative and to take all the necessary measures to reaffirm all Serbian unity, to define a clear and unified national strategy to overcome the existing differences, and to emphasise those things that unite us rather than those that separate us."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Sector for Moral Guidance certainly cannot impose any obligations on the highest state or political leadership, can it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It can't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this passage was not drafted at the Sector for Moral Guidance either. Can you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot agree or disagree. I don't know where this was drafted. But judging by the contents, it does not fall within the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance. I said, yesterday, that this whole sentence could have been copied from some other document. Just look at this bit that goes after "national strategy." "To overcome the existing differences and emphasise the things that unite us rather than those that separate us." That was indeed a distinctive feature of Republika Srpska. All the rest are general phrases that could have been copied from another document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the text that you've just read, and the passage from the other page, there is nothing about raising the -- boosting the morale of the fighting men and the measures that can be taken to do that. That is something that we would logically look for from the Sector for Moral Guidance?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And apart from the heading, "Moral and Psychological Support," there is nothing in this passage that would really be in the purview of the Sector for Moral Guidance. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In preparations made at the Supreme Command for making certain decisions, the president could also have used the intelligence sources from the MUP, that is, the State Security, when he was preparing all sorts of briefs and --

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As the Supreme Commander, it was in his powers to consult whoever he thought was the most qualified to help him with that kind of document, but this kind of document is really something that is best developed by experts. Experts could have produced this kind of directive. That should apply to the entirety of the armed forces, not only the army. But we are now discussing things that were already written, and I apologise if I'm drawing on my experience and knowledge of staff work; although, I've already pointed out I've never seen any of those directives. So in conclusion, the Supreme Commander had the ability to use the services of people who were familiar with the problems and who were able to formulate these matters in summary form without any details. And he would issue that as guidelines, as instructions, for the work of the armed forces, but I don't see that the Ministry of Interior, the police, is included in any way, at least, not as a unit to which assignments are issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Of course, the president would have used the services of people he trusted, not people he was in conflict with. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, I agree. That's a principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, let me move on to another topic. You were examined by the Prosecution yesterday, and you spoke about your meeting with President Karadzic on the 14th of July 1995. Do you agree? Do you remember that? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember discussing that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecution asked you about the persons who were present at the meeting. I will read out a passage from your evidence. They asked you about it in the interview as well, and that is -- it is now correctly recorded. He read to you a passage from your interview, and I'll read to you the next passage on page 39 in my version. I don't know which version you have because there have been some revisions. The Prosecution asked you whether Gvero had been at that meeting with you. Answer, you said: "To be frank, I don't remember." Do you recall giving that answer to the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No verbal response]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then a little further below, line 26, he asked you: "General, try hard to remember. Was Gvero at that meeting or not?" And you replied: "I really can't remember. You should ask Gvero if he remembers." That was your answer to the Prosecution, if you remember.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I answered and I stand by this statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that, when you met again with the Prosecution here, you spoke to them and you said that you believed Gvero had not been at that meeting. Do you remember saying that during the proofing? And we know that from the proofing notes we received.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, I said to the Prosecutor that upon subsequent reflection and logical thinking, I had come to the conclusion that General Gvero was not present at the meeting. During the interview, I could not remember exactly whether he was or whether he wasn't. I still can't remember, but I concluded that, in view of the job that I had there, he could not have been present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown P2905? Scroll down a little, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, in the interview, you also said to the Prosecutor this was not the only time that you met with Karadzic, is that correct, that that was not the only meeting that you had with him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you said that General Gvero was with you only on one occasion, and that he introduced you as Colonel Skrbic upon your arrival at the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's exactly what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the document and please find your name and the time that you spent in that meeting. This is a list of the visitors who, on the 14th of July 1995, had appointments with President Karadzic, and your name is among them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt. Can I just ask what my friend quoted on page 24, line 15: "And you said that General Gvero was with you only on one occasion, and they introduce you as Colonel Skrbic upon your arrival at the Main Staff." Is that being represented as being in the proofing note? I wasn't sure what he was quoting or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic would know. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is my mistake actually. One part of that is in the witness's notes and the other part arises from the interview, on one page of the interview. On page 34 and 35 in B/C/S, I found this information, when Gvero said, "General, this is Colonel Skrbic." --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: "President, this is Colonel Skrbic."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So I quoted both sources.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, on the 14th of July 1995, you were not colonel; you were general; is that correct.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and it says so in the notebook. It says "General Skrbic." I was promoted on the 23rd of June 1995. That's when I became general.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, only the names can be found in this list. If General Gvero had been with you, his name would be there?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree, and you can look at the time, 12.15 to 12.36. Hardly enough room for two generals there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And when he introduced you as Colonel, that was when you arrived at the Main Staff. Would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my first meeting with the president. I don't know who asked me about that, whether the Prosecutor or some of the Defence counsel, and I said that the first time I met with the president was when General Gvero introduced me to him and said, "Mr. President, this is Colonel Skrbic, the assistant commander for moral guidance and personnel matters. He had joined us from the 2nd Krajina Corps."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was immediately upon your arrival at the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In 1994? You joined the Main Staff in 1994, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General, sir. You already spoke about President Karadzic's opinion of General Gvero, when president said that he was not an old lady and that he would remove General Gvero. Do you remember saying that in your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that I said that to the Prosecutor in my attempt to interpret the words that were said to me by the president at that moment. Do you want me to repeat?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify. The way I understood you was that President Karadzic said for himself that he was not an old lady and that he had an intention to remove General Gvero from his position, and that was to show his strict attitude towards General Gvero; at least, that's what I understood.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impression was just that. He was telling me how he would act strictly with all the generals and that he would flex muscle with them, primarily with General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you joined the Main Staff and when you settled in, could you tell us something about the relationship between General Gvero and President Karadzic? The Prosecutor asked you something about that and he asked you whether President Karadzic was angry with General Gvero, and you said that: "Yes, that happened very often." Can you explain? Can you elaborate upon your words?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to expand a little bit on that. I'll try to be as short as possible. If the Court will allow me, I'll try and be as brief as possible, but it will take some time to. In Republika Srpska, officers were often referred to as communists by a lot of people, or commies.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I apologise. I need to interrupt you here. I'm asking you very concretely about General Gvero, only about General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you will allow me, I know what your question was, but I have to make a short introduction. It won't take long. President believed that General Gvero was the main commie, the principal commie. He thought that he was an Orthodox MPV. Let me explain the abbreviation MPV. An MPV stands for something that was known in the JNA as "moral and political education," which was one subject in the education of soldiers. So those who were teaching that were MPVs. President Karadzic also used the derogatory terms for Gvero. He called him a red plague, the devil of the Main Staff, somebody who was stalling the work of the Main Staff. So, really, I was puzzled at times when I heard that, and I was wondering how come he did not proceed and to remove him. And the conflicts between the two of them went even deeper on two very specific issues. The first of these issues was the fact that General Gvero wanted to uphold the constitution and did not want to politicise the army; whereas, the president wanted to appoint assistant commanders for moral guidance in all levels, only members of the SDS, of the Serbian Democratic party. Only those people were to be appointed assistant commanders for morale by President Karadzic. And the third issue that was a sticking point between the two of them, which actually broke the camel's back, was the fact that the president wanted to monopolise all information about the army and its activities, and to remove the issuance of information from the framework of the army and place it within a civilian body. I apologise. One more thing that I need to say. I just need to explain what I mean when I say "information." I mean informing the general public about the army and the activities of the army. It's something in the West would be referred as "porte parole" or something to that effect. In the army, we called it "informing."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that's why he established a press centre with his daughter, Sonja Karadzic, at its head in order to provide exclusive information. Do you remember that press centre was established in Pale?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of that. To be honest, there were stories to that effect, but I don't remember. There were stories that he had done that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And he was going to replace General Gvero with Miroslav Deronjic. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He wanted to appoint a civilian instead of General Gvero. I'm not sure that it was Deronjic; but if you say so, I don't have a reason not to believe you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Deronjic was an SDS politician; he was not a soldier?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was an Orthodox SDS member. He was not a soldier, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown Exhibit number 6D137?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, this is a letter by President Karadzic sent to General Gvero. The date, as you can see, is the 18th of December 1994. Could you please read the passage on the bullet point 1, and see what Karadzic says to Gvero in this letter? Can you do it aloud, please?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the document the first time during the proofing for my testimony, and now I see it for the second time. I'm reading the bullet point 1: "In your first sentence, you have refuted yourself because it ambiguously confirms that you do not respect the institution of the President of the Republic and the Supreme Commander, let alone the person who is currently discharging those duties."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, does this letter show the essence of the relationship between General Gvero and President Karadzic during the period between 1994 and the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only partially, because their relationship was even worse than the document shows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, sorry to interrupt, Your Honour, but just to clarify, the Prosecution did not show this document to the witness. The witness said during his proofing, he was shown this for the first time. I didn't want the Court to be under the impression this was something -- just to be clear, it's not something that we used or showed to him. It was shown to him by my friend, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Nicholls. Perhaps, Mr. Krgovic, you could clarify that with the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, the first time you saw this document was when I met up with you here in The Hague, with the approval of the Prosecutor, and I showed you this document?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I said that I -- that Counsel Krgovic had shown the document to me, only after the approval was given by the Prosecutor for Counsel Krgovic to get in touch with me, and this was here, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, we've gone through this before, and no disrespect to the witness or my friend. We don't approve or disapprove any meetings. Mr. Krgovic told me that he would like to meet with the witness and I said I would convey that to the witness, and I told the witness, "Various counsel would like to meet with you. That is entirely up to you. Can I give them your mobile phone number?" And he, "Yes." I don't approve or disapprove of any meetings with witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that explanation which we knew already about. Yes, Mr. Krgovic. Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Agreement, let's say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question, and we'll have a break in about two minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Skrbic, do you know the occasion after which this document was issued? Do you know anything about Spasoje Zeljkovic, the assistant commander for Moral Guidance in the brigade?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in the 2nd Krajina Corps, I knew Spasoje Zeljkovic personally. I believe that he was an assemblyman in the Assembly. I don't know whether he was appointed the assistant commander for Morale in Grahovo or something similar, and I can't remember whether that gave rise to this document. I can't remember. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, would this be a good time for our break?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honours, I misspoke. It has nothing to do with this witness. At the very beginning of the hearing, the next witness, Witness 4, I said he would be available as well tomorrow. I've been told he is not available tomorrow. He won't be here tomorrow. Sorry for that. He's available today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You will face us with the same problems that you faced us last week, on the basis of which we agreed with you that we should not proceed with the hearing of his evidence in hiccups.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: In that case, I will go through with him whatever time is left today. I will be happy to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So Mr. Krgovic, let's proceed and try to conclude as well, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I must inform the Court that my cross-examination will take a bit longer than I had originally announced for two reasons: Reason 1 is that a subject had been opened up in the examination-in-chief that I had not planned to examine on, and that's the issue of directives. The second reason is your decision concerning my client directly. We have in front of us a man who has assistant for Moral Guidance in the corps and who performed similar duties as my client. He can tell us about the document that the Court decided to admit, and that is the reason why my examination will take a bit longer; that is, at least another hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are a patient lot, Mr. Krgovic, so go ahead. We'll not treat you any differently than we did treat Mr. Petrusic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General, you saw this heading. Isn't it a bit unusual for the president of the republic and the Supreme Commander to address directly General Gvero in this way? What is the usual line of communication between a subordinate officer and the president of the republic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The president of the republic may address anyone he wishes, and there are no restrictions on him in that way, but to leave a written trace on the violation of regulations is something that is a great surprise to me. Something like this should have been done through the commander of the Main Staff who is his immediate subordinate, rather than addressing a commander within the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But that is something that was frequently done by the president; at least, as far as General Gvero is concerned.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regrettably, he violated a regulation and left a written trace of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned two reasons why General Gvero and President Karadzic were in conflict, but do you know about the argument that arose between them when Gvero enabled the transport of Muslim General Hodzic from Republika Srpska to Belgrade for treatment? He was called Yugo-nostalgic, a partisan of brotherhood and unity, and that even gave rise to a programme on the radio and television of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought it was General Emil Sarac, but now I hear you say you say it was General Hodzic who went to the Military Medical Academy in Belgrade, because General Gvero made that possible. He suffered criticism from the president of the republic for doing that humane thing, and that happened on an idealogical level where they seemed to diverge very deeply.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry. Could we just have a date or time frame?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. We've heard other evidence on this, but, Mr. Krgovic, could you put it within a time frame, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned 1994, in fact, although it's not on the record, and I believe the witness heard me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: General, was it in 1994?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I really don't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Was it after you came to the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, do you know that as a result of this conflict, the National Assembly of Republika Srpska recommended or decided that General Gvero should no longer be in active military service, the same as General Boric, General Djukic, and Lieutenant-Colonel Milutinovic? That was sometime in April 1995, at the Sanska Assembly session.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that it was at a session of the National Assembly, that it was proposed that these generals be retired, but their retirement was not in the hands of the National Assembly. It was in the hands of the president of the republic, and, of course, he didn't do that. However, the public at large in Republika Srpska was informed of that proposal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What was the reaction of General Mladic to this conflict and the ever-more frequent demands that General Gvero be replaced?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The commander of the Main Staff, General Mladic, marginalised, sidelined, General Gvero, to protect him from that unpleasantness, so that General Gvero did not perform but a part of the duties that were actually in his purview. For instance, I would go to a session of the government or the Assembly when legal documents regarding the army were discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What about meetings with the highest state leadership? Tolimir or General Milovanovic went to attend these rather than General Gvero, or maybe some other officers?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When there were sessions of the Supreme Command and people from the Main Staff were invited to attend, sometimes only the commander went, sometimes all of us assistants went. I don't remember whether General Gvero was left out later.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As a consequence, was General Gvero transferred from Crna Rijeka to Han Pijesak at one point?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He did move to Han Pijesak, to the office where I had room. It was a hotel requisitioned to become some sort of logistical command post, and that's how we referred to it in the war, logistical command post.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But he moved to the cultural hall where the press centre was and only later to the hotel?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm talking about the building that was next to the municipal hall in Han Pijesak, and the press centre was based there throughout the war. For a while, General Gvero was also based there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We are talking about 1995 and the period after the Assembly session in Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We are talking about that period, but I cannot give you the exact dates because I don't recall them. But we are talking about 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, I'll move to another topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I see the answer from the witness, but I wonder if my friend, again, can give us a time frame for when he is saying that General Gvero was not in Crna Rijeka and when he was in Han Pijesak or in the -- this building adjacent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. General, we are still in 1995. What we would like to know when this move from Han Pijesak -- from Crna Rijeka to Han Pijesak or vice versa took place in 1995. Are you in a position to enlighten us on that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, it was in 1995. I'm sure of that, but I can't give you the date because I don't remember it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Krgovic, if you have any material which could help assist the witness in remembering the precise month in 1995 when that happened, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I don't have the document, but the session in Sanski Most was on 28th April 1995, so we are talking about the period between April and the summer 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could we say that it was then in that period that General Gvero moved to the press centre and then to the hotel where you were.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Judging by what was said about General Gvero at the time, all the things that were said about him, I'm surprised he didn't leave Republika Srpska altogether, but he did leave Crna Rijeka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that at that time, in 1995, for these reasons, but also for other reasons, General Gvero offered his resignation to General Mladic and asked to be relieved?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: General Gvero mentioned his resignation to me, and I warned him that a general cannot resign. A general can only make an application for termination of service. General Gvero, nevertheless, told me that he submitted his written resignation; but regardless of this misnomer, such a document never reached the personnel service.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because it was torn up by General Mladic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. Now for a different topic. In July 1995, how many persons responded to the name of "President"? How many persons had the title of President? Give me all their different functions and positions.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Republika Srpska, there were more presidents than there were generals. I'll enumerate them: The president of the National Assembly; the president of the republic; the president of the government; in English, prime minister; presidents of various committees and commissions; presidents of municipalities. I believe there were over 50 municipalities in Republika Srpska. Let me leave out the presidents of local communes because in wartime they did not amount to much, in terms of power. That's a large number of presidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Biljana Plavsic, member of the Presidency, and Nikola Koljevic, member of the Presidency, would they be among those?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were vice-presidents. They were vice-presidents. But I was personally present during a conversation between General Gvero and Mr. Nikola Koljevic, who was an expert on Shakespeare, on a European level, when General Gvero addressed him as President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General Gvero held Mr. Koljevic in great esteem?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Great, indeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Greater than President Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would rather not answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness Exhibit P1096B?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There will be no broadcast of this document, as it is confidential, I'm told. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the lower part of the page, please, the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you've probably had no occasion to see this document before. This is an intercept, an intercepted conversation, between General Gvero and Karadzic, allegedly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we see the next page?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Read carefully these two intercepts, please, to yourself.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: From beginning to end?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Have you read it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, only the title of the president is mentioned in the intercept. The other details are not mentioned, and you can't hear the president. His voice is not recorded in the intercept. This friendly exchange and the relationship full of respect between the collocutors would not reflect the relationship that General Gvero and President Karadzic in July. Do you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That would be my conclusion as well. This is a very correct exchange.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will no longer need this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, sir, you joined the Republika Srpska army in 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And you were appointed the assistant for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs in the 2nd Krajina Corps; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My commander in the 2nd Krajina Corps was General Grujo Boric.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Up to the moment when you were transferred to the Main Staff, that is?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you a document which originates from 1992 and concerns partly the organ that you were a member of.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 6D129? Can the witness please be shown the bottom part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is a document signed by General Gvero.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we now go back to the beginning of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the second paragraph; i.e., could you please read the entire paragraph starting with number 1?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Shall I read aloud, the first paragraph? "In our previous documents, on several occasions, we have drawn the attention to the need to prevent retaliation against the innocent population, plunder, arson, destruction, and ill treatment. Such actions are not and should not be characteristic of the members of our army because they tarnish the reputation and the moral figure of the Serbian soldier. We cannot allow the incorrect and vindictive behaviour and actions against the innocent and powerless population whose only fault is the fact that they are not Serbs." I've read out the first paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we scroll down a little bit, because there is another paragraph in the document that I would like to show to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the part that begins with the words, "for that reason"?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading: "For that reason, it is necessary, within the next period of time, to pay a lot more attention to this activity. With this regard, the attitude towards local and foreign journalists, representatives of UNPROFOR, the ICRC, and other international organisations has to be warm, humane, and extremely correct. Their requests to have been met at all times. Their work has to be facilitated, and they have to be won over as much as possible."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, when you joined the army of Republika Srpska, were there the positions that you heard from General Gvero, the positions that he himself applied in his work?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Since I joined the 2nd Krajina Corps somewhat later, I remember that I found that document there. My predecessor, Colonel Galic, whose name I believe was Marko, handed it over to me. Not only based on this document, but also on the basis of some actions and the advice that we received from the organ for morale, I can say that this topic was always mentioned, not as the main topic but this topic was on the agenda all the time. I have also shown you the propaganda material of the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, we'll come to that.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's a part of the same topic, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that topic, but I will introduce it in a somewhat different way.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very well, then. Go on.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: During your interview with the Prosecutor in Belgrade, you said, and I quote from page 43: "General Gvero distributed the propaganda material to the ICRC from Geneva in Serbian dealing with the treatment of prisoners of war and the wounded. While I was a member of the 2nd Krajina Corps, I also received such material. If I'm able to locate it, I will bring it to you." Indeed, you brought that material with you and handed it over to the Prosecutor when you arrived in The Hague; am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I brought the material. I was fortunate enough to be able to find it in my library, which is rather rich. Fortunately enough, I found it; and since I made that promise, I brought it with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown 6D143? This document should be in e-court, but I've been informed that there is some problems with the downloading from the e-court. That's why we prepared hard copies. Unfortunately, the document is in Serbian only. It has not been translated because we received it from the Prosecutor's Office only yesterday. That's why I would kindly ask the usher to place the document on the ELMO. I could give my copy to the witness because in my copy the chapters are marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just that I have the originals here which the witness gave to us on Saturday, if he would prefer the witness to use the originals.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do you agree to that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's use the originals, and thank you, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we also have it on the ELMO? Could you put on the ELMO the rule of behaviour for the troops?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, could you please describe the documents to the Trial Chamber, the contents of the documents?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the first image?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm referring to all the documents, if you could do it in a short outline?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: These are all documents of the ICRC from Geneva translated into Serbian. There is a calendar there with some images.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As you're talking about the document, can you place it on the ELMO so that all of us are able to follow?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Look at this document and the images here. Inside is a calendar for 1993 and 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Go back to the title page.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says here, "Respect and protect the sick and the wounded opponents." Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Do you want me to read everything?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'll do it for you, to save the time. Can you go on and show us the next document? These are the rules of behaviour for the troops. The next document, please? This is, "Who are we? Delegates of the International Committee of the Red Cross," speaking of the role of the International Committee of the Red Cross; am I right?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The next document, please. This is another brochure of the International Committee of the Red Cross, speaking about the role of the International Red Cross. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, also its history, its founders, some basic information about the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And this document. These are the fundaments of the rules of war?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, intended for the officers. And you can see here it says, "Summary for the officers, the rules of combat, and the programme of training." This is just an excerpt from a textbook authored by F. Demulinej [phoen], about the rules of war for armed forces. Again, the brochure was published by the International Committee of the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, General. One question now: When you mentioned the propaganda material, in the English language, this word "propaganda" has a somewhat different meaning than notice Serbian language. Its usage is somewhat different in English than it is in the Serbian. Let me just put it this way: This would be affirmative material dealing with the conveyance of information with the intention to exert positive influence on the Serbian soldiers and with the intention to teach them how to deal with the prisoners of war in keeping with the international conventions?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, the word "propaganda" does not have a negative connotation here, but rather a positive connotation. It asserts to reaffirm some positions that are put forth in all of these brochures; would I be correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We called the material "propaganda" without referring to its contents. In the West, this would be called marketing or something to that effect. In other words, the word "propaganda" in the Serbian language does not have a negative connotation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And General Gvero gave you all this to distribute among the troops and to inform them about the contents of all that material?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. He sent all that material to us. He did not give it to us personally. He sent it to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then you went on and distributed all that?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not have enough copies for everybody, so the material intended for the officers was given only to the officers, and the rest was given to the troops. Let me tell you exactly what was given to the officers: The basics of the rules of war. That's what was given to the officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honours. I haven't been completely alert and following which documents are being referred to and put on the ELMO. I just wonder for a clear record if these should be marked as he talks. They are in B/C/S so I can't read them. Perhaps, it will be completely clear when they are translated what is being referred to. It's not a criticism. It's just something that occurred to me as I saw him put something on the ELMO and then take it away and talk about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What I suggest, Mr. Krgovic, is that you prepare a document, after you've finished with your cross-examination, in which these documents are described and given a reference number, and I think we can deal with that in that way. It shouldn't be difficult for you. I mean, it's all in Cyrillic script, and it's difficult for us to follow.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We sent these documents for translation. They are in e-court. But for some technical difficulties, the pages have not been marked. I will, therefore, follow your instructions, and I will prepare the documents in the way you asked me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The important thing is that if later on at any point in time we need to go through this transcript and understand exactly which documents you're referring to or you have been and the witness have been referring to, we can make some sense out of it, because otherwise, Mr. Nicholls is correct, there will be utter confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. If you already know in your mind which 65 ter number or which exhibit number you are going to assign to these documents, then perhaps, as you go along and you refer the witness to any one of these documents, you may just add, "This document will be assigned Exhibit number so and so," and that will help us.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. We gave this document number 6D143.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But that doesn't help much, because if they are going to be accumulated together in one document, it still leaves the possibility for confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We will observe this instruction, and we will properly mark all these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Let's proceed then. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: General, a moment ago, answering my question, you said you performed the duties of assistant commander for Moral Guidance in the 2nd Krajina Corps. You were in that position from your arrival to the army of Republika Srpska until the time you went to the Main Staff to become assistant for Mobilisation, to shorten the name of that body. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct. If necessary, I can repeat to the Court how it was called. It was Sector for Mobilisation, Organisation, and Personnel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I will now show you one document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Your Honours. P2512.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at this document. If you wish, I can give you a copy, a hard copy, because I wanted to go through a couple of details with you. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The title is, "Jurisdiction and filling of vacancies in the organ for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs." It deals with the jurisdiction of this organ in units. To which units does this organ apply?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Units from the rank -- from the level of battalion up to the level of the Main Staff, but only organs for Moral Guidance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't apply to the Main Staff itself, only the subordinated units?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course. The Main Staff stipulates the jurisdiction. It doesn't need to tell itself what its duties are.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And it stipulates how vacancies are to be filled in lower units?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not really the topic of this document because the filling of vacancies is a problem in the purview of my sector. But they did express, as far as I can see, some of their own wishes, as if they had not taken into account establishment. Establishment prescribes it all. It is year 1995. They had to reorganise the army and they had to prepare the material in order to fill the units in brigades, battalions, et cetera, but they had to prepare the units. Officers were in short supply, even for operations and other important duties, and they thought to themselves, "We can't waste them on Moral Guidance."

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this document was never implemented in practice?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which part are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I mean the part that concerns personnel.

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. In terms of personnel, it was not implemented. As far as these general sentences are concerned, these are ideal prototypes that were sometimes not attained in wartime. And there is probably a discrepancy, the kind of discrepancy that exists between school textbooks and what happens in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you look at one passage, the one that concerns cooperation with the authorities and other social entities, enterprises, and institutions? Look at the last item, DJ. It says, "In keeping with the positions instructions and orders from superior commands, there is to be cooperation with UNPROFOR and other humanitarian organisations." You were assistant for Moral Guidance on corps level. Did you perform these duties that I've just read out?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I, as assistant commander for Moral Guidance, Religious, and Legal Affairs, did not perform these duties. It was the Chief of Staff who did that, the Chief of Staff in the command of the 2nd Krajina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Towards the beginning on the same page, there is a passage that says, "Shall have close cooperation with intelligence..."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel read slowly or indicate what he's reading?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise to the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And what page it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's page 4 in my version. In e-court, it's 5. Sorry, it's 5 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've seen this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perform these duties at any time?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is an instruction that stipulates how to collect information for the purposes of psychological and propaganda activities, but we had neither material nor personnel capacities to ever organise that kind of activity. We tried only to protect our fighting men from propaganda; but regrettably, even in that, we were not particularly successful.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: While you were assistant for Moral Guidance, what kind of resources did you have? Did you have men at your disposal? How did it work? What exactly did you do?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't bring that notebook that I had yesterday. I came to the 2nd Krajina Corps and brought that notebook and one pencil. That's all I had in terms of material resources. I had one journalist, one cameraman who brought his own camera, to make video footage and inform our public. And whenever we had enough petrol, we sent that to the radio show which was called, "At the Ramparts of the Home Land." Sometimes when we didn't have petrol, we didn't do that. But it was all very superficial because we did not have the capacity to get real indicators of the state of morale in our units. We also attended funerals and that was one of the hardest duties we had. Once, in Drvar, I attended two funerals; in Glamoc, another two. And there were five in total. That's the kind of duties we performed. I won't go into specifics. Of course, we always attended senior staff meetings of corps commanders because we were directly subordinated to the commander of the corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you didn't interfere in command, and you had nothing to do with the execution of military operations?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Everything that was discussed at this senior staff meeting, in the office of the corps commander, was covered by a particular person; and, thus, our task was to report to the commander on issues that are listed in this document as well but on a much smaller scale, but we did not have the personnel capacities or material capacities.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When you were an assistant, you were directly subordinated to the commander and you reported to him?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I didn't send any reports to the Main Staff - I was not allowed to, and I did not - without the knowledge of the corps commander, and that's how it was in all corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in lower units?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, General. I will now take up another subject you discussed with the Prosecution yesterday. It concerns certain documents you were shown in examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we show the witness P0013? Can we see the lower part of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the signature. We have in print, "Assistant Minister, Momcilo Kovacevic." It's typewritten, and then we have in longhand, "for," and somebody else's signature. Do you see it?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: When such a document is sent by teletype, and when the incoming telegram is received, the recipient would only see the typewritten part, and they would not see the word "for" and the signature, correct?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the recipient would conclude that this was signed by the assistant minister?

utterances.speaker: PETAR SKRBIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. If you allow me to make a link with our discussion yesterday about standing in for or acting on behalf of, this is the correct way to sign: To put the word "for" in front of whosever function, and it was signed by Di Capa Tinja [phoen]; and after the word "minister," they added the proper suffix to indicate the noun case. But the teletypist would not type that, if my knowledge of communication is still fresh.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
